offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life
physical_harm: No injuries on the body of deceased; death was alleged to be caused by compelling the deceased to consume poison
number_of_offences: Three offences charged, two upheld (304B and 498A)
motive: Dowry harassment and demand for money
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the concurrent finding by the courts below that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty as explained under Section 498A IPC, and that the deceased died an unnatural death based on the prosecution's case, though the medical evidence was found to be insufficient for the dowry death charge under Section 304B IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, believing their evidence that the deceased used to complain about harassment for dowry by the accused.

legal_representation.accused: Mohit Kumar Shah, Rituraj Choudhary, Shilpi Shah, Navin Prakash

investigation_status: Charge sheet filed on 2.11.1994, post-mortem report not produced, forensic lab report not produced
procedural_irregularity: Investigating Officer failed to secure viscera report, public prosecutor failed to guide investigating officer, magistrate failed to apply mind

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted of offences under sections 304B and 498A IPC
appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeal in part, acquitted the surviving accused of the offence under section 304B IPC

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused harassed the deceased for dowry and forced her to commit suicide by consuming poison, leading to her unnatural death. They relied on the FIR and the testimony of witnesses to establish the harassment and the cause of death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the conviction under Section 304B IPC was not supported by legal material, as the post-mortem report and forensic laboratory report regarding the examination of viscera were not produced, and there was no direct evidence of poisoning or unnatural death.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that for a conviction under Section 304B IPC, the prosecution must establish that the death was due to burns, bodily injury, or occurred otherwise than under normal circumstances, and that the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment for dowry demands.
precedent_relied_upon: Bhupendra v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2013(3) SCALE 552
